screens.title: Implementing and Managing NTP with Chrony
screens.narratorSegment: Accurate time is an infrastructure foundation. In this lesson you will learn why synchronized clocks matter for log correlation, security protocols like Kerberos, and certificate validation. We will focus on Chrony, the modern NTP implementation used on RHEL 8 and later. You will see how chronyd queries upstream sources, how chronyc reports synchronization state, and practical server and client configurations for secure, resilient timekeeping. We will also cover authentication with symmetric keys, the difference between slewing and stepping, and common troubleshooting steps such as checking firewall rules and interpreting chronyc output. A clear, correct time source prevents replay attacks, improves incident timelines, and ensures distributed services agree on event order. By the end, you will be able to configure chronyd as a client or server, validate synchronization with chronyc, and implement authentication and firewall changes safely. Consider how an inaccurate clock might complicate a security investigation or break authentication — that risk is the reason we standardize time across servers.

screens.title: Why accurate time matters
screens.narratorSegment: Accurate time is not cosmetic; it is functional. Timestamps enable correlation across distributed logs so you can trace a request or incident end to end. When clocks diverge, log entries cannot be reliably ordered, making debugging and forensics much harder. Security protocols such as Kerberos depend on limited clock skew to prevent replay attacks — if clocks are too far apart, authentication fails. Certificates and token validity also rely on coherent clocks, so a wrong system time can cause services to reject valid certificates or allow expired ones to appear valid. In practice, that means a single misconfigured server can break access for an entire application stack or destroy the audit trail you need during an investigation. The concrete example to keep in mind is a multi-host authentication failure: if a client and KDC disagree on time by several minutes, the client’s request will be rejected. A common misconception is that occasional small drift is harmless — in reality, even a few seconds can confuse sequencing and security checks in distributed systems. The takeaway is simple: plan reliable, authenticated time sources and verify them regularly so logs, authentication, and certificates remain trustworthy.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Why accurate time matters
Definition

Consistent timestamps and security

Timestamps let you sequence events across machines and validate time-sensitive protocols. When clocks disagree, both operational and security features break.

Concrete example
If a client’s clock is minutes ahead of a Kerberos KDC, authentication fails because tickets appear not yet valid or expired.
Common misconception
Small drift is harmless. Even second-level drift can confuse log ordering and certificate validation in distributed systems.
Why it matters
  • Log correlation: consistent timestamps let you rebuild event sequences across nodes.
  • Security: Kerberos and other auth methods reject requests beyond acceptable clock skew.
  • Certificates: validity periods depend on accurate system clocks to accept or reject certs.
Key Takeaway

Make time part of your security and observability plan. Verify sources and monitor offsets to keep systems trustworthy.

screens.title: Chrony vs ntpd
screens.narratorSegment: Chrony is the modern choice on RHEL 8+ for a reason. Chrony synchronizes faster, recovers from large offsets more efficiently, and handles intermittent network connectivity and virtual machine pauses better than the older ntpd. In virtualized environments, guests can be suspended and later resumed, producing large clock jumps. ntpd typically tries to 'slew' the clock slowly which can be too slow or ineffective for large drifts. Chrony, however, can step the clock when needed or apply sophisticated slewing strategies to correct time quickly. A concrete example: a VM resumed after migration might be seconds or minutes off; chronyd can reach accurate time faster, reducing authentication failures and log inconsistencies. A common misconception is that both implementations are interchangeable in behavior — in practice their handling of large offsets and unstable networks differs significantly. The practical takeaway is to standardize on chrony for modern, dynamic infrastructures because it provides more predictable, faster convergence and better resilience when network conditions or host state change. Chrony vs ntpd means chrony offers faster synchronization and better handling of vms and intermittent networks than ntpd, making it the recommended default on rhel.. In practical terms, why rhel prefers chrony in modern environments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Chrony vs ntpd
Comparison

Behavior differences

  • Faster convergence: chronyd can reach accurate time quickly using iburst and aggressive adjustments.
  • VM resilience: handles suspensions, migrations, and intermittent networking better than ntpd.
  • Large offsets: chronyd can step the clock when necessary instead of only slewing slowly.
Concrete scenario
A host resumed from a snapshot is several minutes ahead. With ntpd you may wait many minutes for slewing to correct time; chronyd can step or apply faster adjustments so authentication and logging resume correctly.
Common misconception
Assuming ntpd and chrony behave the same. Their algorithms and default behaviors differ, so prefer chrony on RHEL 8+ for cloud and VM workloads.
Key Takeaway

Standardize on chrony for dynamic environments. Its faster adjustments improve reliability and security.

screens.title: chronyd modes and responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: chronyd can play three practical roles: client, server, or peer. As a client, chronyd queries upstream servers or pools to learn the correct time and then adjusts the local clock. Client configuration typically lists pool or server directives in /etc/chrony. conf and uses iburst to speed the initial sync. As a server, chronyd accepts requests from clients on the local network when ntpserve is enabled and appropriate allow directives are present; the server should have reliable upstream references and firewall openings for UDP port 123. As a peer, two chronyd instances may mutually synchronize when both consider each other at equal standing. A concrete example: a server in an isolated site might set local stratum 10 and ntpserve so local clients still get time when upstream sources are unreachable; this is a fallback but must be used with caution because it makes the server authoritative without external validation. A common mistake is forgetting to use allow for internal clients or to open UDP 123 in the firewall, which prevents client synchronization. Understanding these modes lets you design whether a host should pull time, provide it, or collaborate as a peer.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › chronyd modes
Definition

Client, Server, Peer

Each mode declares how chronyd gets or provides time. Choose the mode based on network topology and reliability of upstream sources.

Client
Queries upstream pool/server entries and adjusts local clock. Use iburst for faster initial sync.
Server
Provides time to network clients when ntpserve is enabled and allow directives permit access.
Peer
Mutual synchronization between peers when equal trust is desired.
Configuration highlights
Key chrony.conf directives include pool/server, allow for client access, ntpserve to enable server mode, and local stratum to stand in when upstream sources are unreachable. Also set driftfile and logdir for stability and logging.
Common mistake
Enabling server features without opening UDP 123 or without proper allow directives prevents clients from actually connecting. Always verify firewall rules and restart chronyd after changes.
Key Takeaway

Decide the role based on topology: clients pull, servers provide with ntpserve, and peers synchronize mutually when needed.

keyIdea.title: Configure carefully
keyIdea.text: Edit /etc/chrony.conf to select sources, enable server functionality correctly, and use iburst, driftfile, and logdir for reliable operation.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › chrony.conf directives
Code example
# /etc/chrony.conf (client example)
pool 2.rhel.pool.ntp.org iburst
pool 0.centos.pool.ntp.org iburst

# Allow NTP client access from local network
allow 192.168.1.0/24

# Write current time drift
driftfile /var/lib/chrony/drift

# Log time adjustments
logdir /var/log/chrony
Use iburst for fast startup. Set driftfile so chronyd remembers hardware drift between reboots and logdir to capture adjustments.
Server example
# /etc/chrony.conf (server example)
pool 2.rhel.pool.ntp.org iburst
allow 192.168.100.0/24
local stratum 10
ntpserve
Remember to open UDP 123 in the firewall and restart chronyd. local stratum acts as a fallback authoritative source when no upstream servers are available.
Key Takeaway

Edit chrony.conf carefully, restart chronyd, and verify with chronyc to confirm the host behaves as client or server as intended.

screens.title: Verifying with chronyc
screens.narratorSegment: chronyc is the primary tool for monitoring and debugging chronyd. The command chronyc sources lists time sources with a State column that shows symbols like ^ for server and = for peer — these symbols help you determine where the host is getting time. Look at Offset to see the current difference between your clock and the reference; a low offset means good accuracy. chronyc tracking reports reference ID, stratum, and last offset which tells you the host’s synchronization health. Stratum indicates distance from a primary time reference: 1 is a primary source while higher numbers are farther down the hierarchy. chronyc activity shows how many sources are online or offline and can reveal reachability problems. A concrete example is when chronyc sources reports State as? meaning unreachable: the immediate troubleshooting steps are to check firewall rules for UDP 123 and verify network connectivity to the configured pool/server addresses. A common trap is interpreting a nonzero offset as an immediate emergency — small offsets are normal, but persistent high offsets indicate network issues or unreliable sources. Use chronyc repeatedly while you apply fixes to confirm progress.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Verifying with chronyc
Example commands
chronyc sources -v
# Shows State, Offset, Stratum, and reference

chronyc tracking
# Shows reference ID, stratum, last offset, and overall sync status

chronyc activity
# Shows number of online/offline sources
Run these commands after restarting chronyd and after changes. Repeat them while troubleshooting to confirm reachability and offset improvements.
Read the output
  • State: ^ server, = peer, ? unreachable — use this to identify why sources aren’t used.
  • Offset: difference in seconds; low is good, persistent high needs action.
  • Stratum: 1 is primary, higher values mean further away from a reference clock.
Troubleshooting step
If State is ?, check UDP 123 is allowed and validate network connectivity to the configured servers or pools.
Key Takeaway

chronyc commands give you the health of synchronization. Learn to interpret State, Offset, and Stratum to act quickly.

screens.title: Configuring chronyd as a server
screens.narratorSegment: When configuring a host as an NTP server, start with reliable upstream sources. Use pool or server directives to reference public pools or dedicated stratum-1 or stratum-2 servers. Enable ntpserve so the daemon answers client requests and add allow with the clients’ subnet to permit access. The firewall must permit incoming UDP 123; on RHEL use firewall-cmd to add the ntp service and reload. If upstream sources are unreachable, local stratum provides a fallback authoritative value so clients still receive a time source — but this must be used judiciously because it declares the host authoritative without validation. A practical configuration includes pool entries with iburst, allow for the client network, ntpserve, and optionally local stratum 10 for isolated networks. After applying changes, restart chronyd and verify with chronyc sources and tracking. A common operational mistake is enabling ntpserve but forgetting firewall rules, leaving clients unable to reach the server. Plan monitoring so you see when your server loses upstream synchronization and avoid inadvertently propagating incorrect time. Configuring chronyd as a server means provide upstream references, enable ntpserve, open udp 123 in the firewall, and use local stratum only as a cautious fallback.. In practical terms, upstream sources, ntpserve, allow, firewall, and fallback stratum. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Configuring chronyd as a server
Architecture

Server responsibilities

  • Maintain reliable upstream references to public pools or authoritative sources.
  • Answer client requests when ntpserve is enabled and allow permits client subnets.
  • Log adjustments and monitor offsets to avoid serving incorrect time.
Operational checklist
  1. Edit /etc/chrony.conf: add pool/server entries, allow 192.168.x.x/24, ntpserve, and optionally local stratum.
  2. Restart chronyd: sudo systemctl restart chronyd.
  3. Open firewall: sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=ntp && sudo firewall-cmd --reload.
  4. Verify with chronyc sources and chronyc tracking.
Operational pitfall
Using local stratum without monitoring can propagate incorrect time. Reserve local stratum for isolated networks and document its use.
Key Takeaway

Make servers reliable: upstream sources, firewall rules, ntpserve, and monitoring prevent accidental propagation of bad time.

screens.title: Symmetric key authentication
screens.narratorSegment: chrony supports symmetric key authentication which prevents unauthenticated servers from influencing your clock. The typical workflow is to generate a secret key, add a line to /etc/chrony. keys with the key ID, algorithm, and value, protect that file with restrictive permissions, and then reference the key ID in /etc/chrony. conf for the server line. Both client and server must share the same key entry for authentication to succeed. A concrete example: create a key using a secure random generator, add a line such as '1 MD5 your_secret' to /etc/chrony. keys, chmod 600 the file, and configure server 192.168.100.10 key 1 iburst on the client. On the server, ensure the same key ID and value is present. A common mistake is inconsistent key material or incorrect permissions, which prevents authentication. After configuring, restart chronyd on both hosts and verify with chronyc sources — you'll only see authenticated responses when keys match. Authentication reduces the risk of time spoofing and is essential for internal authoritative servers. Symmetric key authentication means use symmetric keys in /etc/chrony.keys, protect the file, and reference the key in chrony.conf to ensure only authenticated sources are trusted.. chrony.keys example

screens.title: Common synchronization issues
screens.narratorSegment: When chronyc shows unreachable sources or high offsets, start with the most common causes. Step one is firewall rules: chronyd uses UDP port 123. If outbound or inbound UDP 123 is blocked, sources will be unreachable. Check the host firewall with firewall-cmd or iptables and add the ntp service if missing. Step two is network connectivity: verify DNS resolution and that the configured pool or server IPs are reachable with ping or traceroute. Step three is configuration errors: check /etc/chrony. conf for typos, ensure server or pool directives are correct, and that /etc/chrony. keys contains the correct key when authentication is used. Persistent high offsets may indicate network jitter, an unreliable upstream source, or virtual machine host timing issues; chrony tolerates jitter better than ntpd, but persistent high offsets require investigating the network path or selecting different sources. A useful command sequence is chronyc sources -v, chronyc tracking, and chronyc activity to collect data points before and after each troubleshooting action. A common misconception is to immediately change sources; prefer verifying firewall and connectivity first because they are the simplest and most frequent root causes.

screens.title: Slewing vs Stepping and makestep
screens.narratorSegment: Chronyd can correct time by slewing or stepping. Slewing adjusts the clock slowly so that the time marches toward the reference without abrupt jumps; this is safe for running services but can be slow when offsets are large. Stepping instantly updates the system clock to match the reference and is useful when a machine has a large initial offset such as after an installation, restore, or VM resume. The makestep directive is a configuration option that tells chronyd under what conditions it should step the clock rather than always slew — for example, it can permit stepping during early boots or when offsets exceed a threshold. A practical scenario: a fresh host with a wildly incorrect clock should use makestep to quickly correct time so authentication and log timestamps become meaningful immediately. A common misconception is to avoid stepping entirely; while caution is needed to avoid sudden changes affecting running processes, stepping is appropriate for correcting large initial errors. The guidance is to use makestep for initial corrections and allow normal slewing for small, continuous adjustments. Slewing vs Stepping and makestep means use makestep to allow stepping for large initial errors; rely on slewing for small continual adjustments to minimize disruption.. In practical terms, how chronyd corrects the clock and when to force a step. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Slewing vs Stepping
Definitions

Slewing: slowly adjust the clock rate so time converges without abrupt jumps. Safe for running services.

Stepping: immediately set the clock to the reference time. Useful for large offsets or initial corrections.

Practical usage

Use makestep to allow one-time stepping under controlled conditions, for example on first boot or when the offset exceeds a configured threshold.

A common scenario is new deployments where immediate correct time is necessary for authentication and logging.

Misconception
Avoiding stepping altogether can delay resolution of large offsets; instead use makestep under controlled circumstances.
Key Takeaway

Balance safety and speed: allow stepping for large corrections, and rely on slewing for small, ongoing adjustments.

screens.title: Operational best practices and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: Design time infrastructure with redundancy and safety in mind. Automate verification steps in your deployment pipeline: after configuration changes restart chronyd and run chronyc tracking and chronyc sources -v, then alert on high offsets or unreachable states. The clear operational principle is to combine redundancy, monitoring, and secure authentication to maintain trustworthy time across your estate. fullNarratorScript:
Accurate time is an infrastructure foundation. In this lesson you will learn why synchronized clocks matter for log correlation, security protocols like Kerberos, and certificate validation. We will focus on Chrony, the modern NTP implementation used on RHEL 8 and later. You will see how chronyd queries upstream sources, how chronyc reports synchronization state, and practical server and client configurations for secure, resilient timekeeping. We will also cover authentication with symmetric keys, the difference between slewing and stepping, and common troubleshooting steps such as checking firewall rules and interpreting chronyc output. A clear, correct time source prevents replay attacks, improves incident timelines, and ensures distributed services agree on event order. By the end, you will be able to configure chronyd as a client or server, validate synchronization with chronyc, and implement authentication and firewall changes safely. Consider how an inaccurate clock might complicate a security investigation or break authentication — that risk is the reason we standardize time across servers.

In this first objectives slide we set clear, practical goals. First, you will understand why accurate time synchronization matters in distributed systems and security. That includes how timestamps affect log correlation, Kerberos authentication, and certificate validation. Second, you will learn to configure chronyd as both a client and as a server, including the key directives in /etc/chrony. conf such as server, pool, allow, driftfile, and iburst. These skills let you make a host synchronize reliably with public pools or serve time to a local network. Third, you will implement chronyd security features: creating symmetric keys, placing them in /etc/chrony. keys, and referencing keys in chrony. conf so only authenticated peers are trusted. Finally, you will troubleshoot and verify: using chronyc sources, chronyc tracking, and chronyc activity to interpret state, offset, and stratum. Each objective combines a specific configuration skill with the reason it matters in operations and security. Throughout the lesson we’ll use concrete examples and command snippets so you can apply these skills in a lab or production environment.

This second objectives slide connects objectives to concrete tasks. For the time-synchronization objective, you will map which hosts need authoritative time and decide whether to use public pools, a dedicated internal server, or a mix. For chronyd configuration, you will edit /etc/chrony. conf to add pool or server lines, set driftfile and logdir, and use iburst to speed initial sync — then restart the chronyd service to apply changes. For authentication, you will generate a symmetric key, place it in /etc/chrony. keys with restrictive permissions, and configure both server and client to reference the key ID so they only trust authenticated responses. For verification and troubleshooting, you will run chronyc sources and chronyc tracking repeatedly, interpret State, Stratum, and Offset, and then take corrective actions such as opening UDP 123 in the firewall or checking network routes. Each task links a specific command or configuration change to why it matters in uptime, security, and auditing. Practicing these steps in a lab will make them repeatable and safe in production.

Accurate time is not cosmetic; it is functional. Timestamps enable correlation across distributed logs so you can trace a request or incident end to end. When clocks diverge, log entries cannot be reliably ordered, making debugging and forensics much harder. Security protocols such as Kerberos depend on limited clock skew to prevent replay attacks — if clocks are too far apart, authentication fails. Certificates and token validity also rely on coherent clocks, so a wrong system time can cause services to reject valid certificates or allow expired ones to appear valid. In practice, that means a single misconfigured server can break access for an entire application stack or destroy the audit trail you need during an investigation. The concrete example to keep in mind is a multi-host authentication failure: if a client and KDC disagree on time by several minutes, the client’s request will be rejected. A common misconception is that occasional small drift is harmless — in reality, even a few seconds can confuse sequencing and security checks in distributed systems. The takeaway is simple: plan reliable, authenticated time sources and verify them regularly so logs, authentication, and certificates remain trustworthy.

Chrony is the modern choice on RHEL 8+ for a reason. Chrony synchronizes faster, recovers from large offsets more efficiently, and handles intermittent network connectivity and virtual machine pauses better than the older ntpd. In virtualized environments, guests can be suspended and later resumed, producing large clock jumps. ntpd typically tries to 'slew' the clock slowly which can be too slow or ineffective for large drifts. Chrony, however, can step the clock when needed or apply sophisticated slewing strategies to correct time quickly. A concrete example: a VM resumed after migration might be seconds or minutes off; chronyd can reach accurate time faster, reducing authentication failures and log inconsistencies. A common misconception is that both implementations are interchangeable in behavior — in practice their handling of large offsets and unstable networks differs significantly. The practical takeaway is to standardize on chrony for modern, dynamic infrastructures because it provides more predictable, faster convergence and better resilience when network conditions or host state change. Chrony vs ntpd means chrony offers faster synchronization and better handling of vms and intermittent networks than ntpd, making it the recommended default on rhel.. In practical terms, why rhel prefers chrony in modern environments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

chronyd can play three practical roles: client, server, or peer. As a client, chronyd queries upstream servers or pools to learn the correct time and then adjusts the local clock. Client configuration typically lists pool or server directives in /etc/chrony. conf and uses iburst to speed the initial sync. As a server, chronyd accepts requests from clients on the local network when ntpserve is enabled and appropriate allow directives are present; the server should have reliable upstream references and firewall openings for UDP port 123. As a peer, two chronyd instances may mutually synchronize when both consider each other at equal standing. A concrete example: a server in an isolated site might set local stratum 10 and ntpserve so local clients still get time when upstream sources are unreachable; this is a fallback but must be used with caution because it makes the server authoritative without external validation. A common mistake is forgetting to use allow for internal clients or to open UDP 123 in the firewall, which prevents client synchronization. Understanding these modes lets you design whether a host should pull time, provide it, or collaborate as a peer.

chronyc is the primary tool for monitoring and debugging chronyd. The command chronyc sources lists time sources with a State column that shows symbols like ^ for server and = for peer — these symbols help you determine where the host is getting time. Look at Offset to see the current difference between your clock and the reference; a low offset means good accuracy. chronyc tracking reports reference ID, stratum, and last offset which tells you the host’s synchronization health. Stratum indicates distance from a primary time reference: 1 is a primary source while higher numbers are farther down the hierarchy. chronyc activity shows how many sources are online or offline and can reveal reachability problems. A concrete example is when chronyc sources reports State as? meaning unreachable: the immediate troubleshooting steps are to check firewall rules for UDP 123 and verify network connectivity to the configured pool/server addresses. A common trap is interpreting a nonzero offset as an immediate emergency — small offsets are normal, but persistent high offsets indicate network issues or unreliable sources. Use chronyc repeatedly while you apply fixes to confirm progress.

When configuring a host as an NTP server, start with reliable upstream sources. Use pool or server directives to reference public pools or dedicated stratum-1 or stratum-2 servers. Enable ntpserve so the daemon answers client requests and add allow with the clients’ subnet to permit access. The firewall must permit incoming UDP 123; on RHEL use firewall-cmd to add the ntp service and reload. If upstream sources are unreachable, local stratum provides a fallback authoritative value so clients still receive a time source — but this must be used judiciously because it declares the host authoritative without validation. A practical configuration includes pool entries with iburst, allow for the client network, ntpserve, and optionally local stratum 10 for isolated networks. After applying changes, restart chronyd and verify with chronyc sources and tracking. A common operational mistake is enabling ntpserve but forgetting firewall rules, leaving clients unable to reach the server. Plan monitoring so you see when your server loses upstream synchronization and avoid inadvertently propagating incorrect time. chrony supports symmetric key authentication which prevents unauthenticated servers from influencing your clock. The typical workflow is to generate a secret key, add a line to /etc/chrony. keys with the key ID, algorithm, and value, protect that file with restrictive permissions, and then reference the key ID in /etc/chrony. conf for the server line. Both client and server must share the same key entry for authentication to succeed. A concrete example: create a key using a secure random generator, add a line such as '1 MD5 your_secret' to /etc/chrony. keys, chmod 600 the file, and configure server 192.168.100.10 key 1 iburst on the client. On the server, ensure the same key ID and value is present. A common mistake is inconsistent key material or incorrect permissions, which prevents authentication. After configuring, restart chronyd on both hosts and verify with chronyc sources — you'll only see authenticated responses when keys match. Authentication reduces the risk of time spoofing and is essential for internal authoritative servers. When chronyc shows unreachable sources or high offsets, start with the most common causes. Step one is firewall rules: chronyd uses UDP port 123. If outbound or inbound UDP 123 is blocked, sources will be unreachable. Check the host firewall with firewall-cmd or iptables and add the ntp service if missing. Step two is network connectivity: verify DNS resolution and that the configured pool or server IPs are reachable with ping or traceroute. Step three is configuration errors: check /etc/chrony. conf for typos, ensure server or pool directives are correct, and that /etc/chrony. keys contains the correct key when authentication is used. Persistent high offsets may indicate network jitter, an unreliable upstream source, or virtual machine host timing issues; chrony tolerates jitter better than ntpd, but persistent high offsets require investigating the network path or selecting different sources. A useful command sequence is chronyc sources -v, chronyc tracking, and chronyc activity to collect data points before and after each troubleshooting action. A common misconception is to immediately change sources; prefer verifying firewall and connectivity first because they are the simplest and most frequent root causes.

Chronyd can correct time by slewing or stepping. Slewing adjusts the clock slowly so that the time marches toward the reference without abrupt jumps; this is safe for running services but can be slow when offsets are large. Stepping instantly updates the system clock to match the reference and is useful when a machine has a large initial offset such as after an installation, restore, or VM resume. The makestep directive is a configuration option that tells chronyd under what conditions it should step the clock rather than always slew — for example, it can permit stepping during early boots or when offsets exceed a threshold. A practical scenario: a fresh host with a wildly incorrect clock should use makestep to quickly correct time so authentication and log timestamps become meaningful immediately. A common misconception is to avoid stepping entirely; while caution is needed to avoid sudden changes affecting running processes, stepping is appropriate for correcting large initial errors. The guidance is to use makestep for initial corrections and allow normal slewing for small, continuous adjustments. Here are the essential terms to remember. NTP is the protocol for clock synchronization across networks. Chrony is the modern NTP implementation on RHEL that includes chronyd, the daemon responsible for synchronization, and chronyc, the command-line tool for monitoring and control. Stratum measures how far a source is from a primary reference: lower is better. Offset is the measured difference between your clock and the reference; monitor it and take action when it remains high.
